reason: Text says 'one is driven to the conjecture that medieval alchemy ... was in the last resort a continuation of the doctrine of the Holy Ghost' — the subject is medieval alchemy as a historical movement, not the opus alchymicum, and the claim is explicitly hedged as a conjecture. Correct form: subject 'medieval alchemy' (or alchemical tradition) with a hedged/conjectural qualifier rather than flat jung-asserts on 'the-opus'.
Verbatim definitional statement: 'The contents of the collective unconscious ... are known as archetypes.' Direction, referents, and claim_type are exact.

Paragraph asserts alchemical projections reflect psychological facts, with Luna the symbol of unconsciousness; 'is-psychic-analogue-of' fairly renders symbol-to-psychic-fact, and 'unconsciousness'/'the unconscious' are interchangeable in Jung's usage here.
'The stag signifies the soul' is stated verbatim within the discussion of Lambspringk's Symbols; claim_type jung-reports-parallel with the named source is exactly right.

'Consciousness enables him to adapt in an orderly way and to check the instincts' — strictly consciousness enables man to check, but the checking capacity is attributed to consciousness itself and contrasted with instinct's compulsiveness; the compression is faithful.

Jung asserts in his own voice that the parable contains 'the primitive motif of the murder or sacrifice of the king for the purpose of renewing his kingly power'; the chapter's Rex is the king in question. The edge survives.

'As we have seen, the filius regius is identical with Mercurius' — a direct, unhedged identity claim in Jung's voice; the stage-specific addition (Mercurial serpent) does not weaken the general identity.

Pordage's quoted letter explicitly names the albification/whitening 'their resurrection, because the white rises up out of the black'; mapping resurrection to Rebirth/Renovatio and typing as jung-quotes-source are both accurate.
'The union of consciousness (Sol) with its feminine counterpart the unconscious (Luna)' — the parenthetical equation is explicit and in Jung's own psychological register.

Khunrath's quoted words identify the Philosophical Stone as 'our King ... regenerated and more than perfect'; the ellipsis omits only the sepulchre imagery without changing sense, and claim_type correctly attributes to Khunrath.

'Adam would then be a quaternarius, as he was composed of red, black, white, and green dust from the four corners' — the conditional 'would then be' is Jung drawing his own inference from legend material he clearly endorses across the section; the quaternity reading is his assertion.

The paragraph reads the bridal-chamber swallowing of the lion as a coniunctio scene and explicitly calls the Beya/Gabricus episode 'a parallel'; using it as amplification material for the coniunctio is what the text does.
'The identification of Malchuth with Luna forms a link with alchemy' is stated directly, grounded in the quoted Vigenerus/Zohar passage; jung-reports-parallel with source is the honest type.
'The unconscious, however, transforms it [the Trinity] into a quaternity' — direct assertion in Jung's own voice with exact referents and direction.

The Queen Mother is explicitly credited with 'her capacity to grant rebirth' and the food is 'just the right food ... to rejuvenate the old king and to give him immortality'; 'renews' is a fair rendering, though the textual figure is strictly the Queen Mother of the Cantilena.
'Dorn's caelum, which corresponded to the stone' — verbatim support for the relation, in Jung's own exposition.

The sentence chain attaches unio mentalis to the one 'who has risked the fight with the dragon and is not overcome by it' — Jung deliberately fuses patient and hero, and the dragon-fighter is the grammatical subject who 'attained what the alchemists called the unio mentalis.'
'Mercurius consists of all conceivable opposites ... but is named a unity' — consisting of opposites while being a unity is precisely embodying the union of opposites.
'The king is essentially synonymous with the sun' — verbatim, unhedged, in Jung's own explanatory voice.

'An assimilation of the Christ-image to his own self, which is the "true man"' asserts the self/true-man identity, of which corresponds-to is a weaker and safe rendering; the chen-yen gloss in the node label is an aggregation matter, not a flaw of this edge.
The Rosarium is reported as saying salt is bitter 'because it comes from the mineral of the sea' — derivation from the sea is preserved (via its mineral), and claim_type plus source are honest.

'The daemonic Lilith seems to be a certain aspect of Adam, for the legend says she was created with him from the same earth' — the interpretive claim is Jung's own with exact referents; the mild 'seems' hedge does not change relation or direction.

The paragraph gives a conditional sequence: union of opposites, 'followed by the death of the product of the union (mortificatio ...) and a corresponding nigredo' — and only in the variant where separation is assumed at the start (otherwise nigredo is the initial state or produced by separatio). 'Produces' overstates a mediated, conditional succession; correct form is coniunctio followed-by mortificatio/nigredo.

'Or, if Sol is the spirit and Luna the body' is conditional, but the claim_type is jung-reports-parallel, which honestly captures that Jung is invoking a standing alchemical equation rather than asserting it as doctrine; the parallel itself is genuinely in the text.

The 'since' clause only coheres if the dark sun of feminine psychology is the animus: it is connected with the father-imago precisely because 'the father is the first carrier of the animus-image.' The correspondence is presupposed and load-bearing in Jung's own sentence, so the edge survives.
'The Rebis or Lapis Philosophorum ... we have no difficulty in recognizing it as a symbol of the self' — direct assertion with exact referents.

'The dragon is clearly the filius macrocosmi and, as such, a parallel figure to Christ' — the parallel is explicit; jung-reports-parallel matches this KG's use of the type for Jung's amplificatory parallels, though the omitted 'and at the same time his rival' is a nuance worth preserving elsewhere.

Claim_type jung-quotes-source is dishonest here: 'Sol is the father of Mercurius' is Jung's interpretive paraphrase — the Tabula Smaragdina says the Sun is father of the 'one thing' and never names Mercurius as the son; Jung supplies that identification. Correct form: jung-reports-source-doctrine/paraphrase of the Tabula, or jung-asserts for the Mercurius identification.

The paragraph is line-by-line exposition of an alchemical poem ('the poem takes Mercurius chiefly as a spirit of light'), so 'it is through his work that Mercurius is freed from his chains' is the poem's doctrine reported by Jung, not a jung-asserts claim; 'his work' is also grammatically ambiguous (adept's opus vs. Mercurius's own working). Correct form: jung-reports-source with the poem as source.

Multiply supported in the paragraph: 'the will needs a supraordinate authority, something like a consciousness of itself,' 'volition presupposes a choosing subject,' and 'we can hardly conceive of will and freedom of choice without consciousness.'
